summary: This bash script implements a blog search function that answers questions about a blog by querying an AnythingLLM workspace (which handles vector embeddings and semantic search). It displays the AI's answer along with clickable source links, then runs a secondary exact-match search on blog frontmatter as a safety net to catch articles the semantic search might have missed.

explanations.14: The colon-equals syntax sets a variable to a default value only if it's not already set — so you can override AI_BLOG_DIR by setting it beforehand, but it falls back to ~/repositories/blog if you don't.
explanations.20: The -z test checks if a string is empty; the :- syntax means 'use this value if the variable is unset or empty', so this line checks whether ANYTHINGLLM_API_KEY exists at all.
explanations.35: The -t 1 test checks whether file descriptor 1 (stdout) is connected to a terminal — this lets the function output fancy hyperlinks when you're at a prompt, but plain text when the output is piped to a file or another command.
explanations.37: The :t zsh parameter expansion gets just the filename part of a path (like /foo/bar.md becomes bar.md), so this prints a shortened version of the URL below the hyperlinked title.
explanations.46: This checks whether an alias named ai-blog-search already exists (the (( $+aliases[...] )) syntax), and if so, removes it before defining the function — otherwise zsh would complain that the function name clashes with the alias.
explanations.67: jq -nc creates a JSON object from scratch without reading input, and --arg defines variables that get substituted into the JSON as $m and $s; RANDOM gives a pseudo-random number so each call gets a unique session ID.
explanations.76: This extracts the .error field from the JSON response, or outputs nothing (empty) if that field doesn't exist, so the script can check whether the API call actually failed.
explanations.86: The .sources[]? accesses the sources array but won't error if it's missing, then the select filters to only keep entries whose chunkSource starts with link://, and unique_by removes duplicates based on URL.
explanations.95: The ${(f)sources} zsh syntax splits the string on newlines into array elements so the for loop processes each line separately.
explanations.96: The ${...%%*} and ${..#*} are zsh string slicing — the first takes everything before the tab character, the second takes everything after it, effectively splitting the tab-separated fields.
explanations.133: This splits the question into words, lowercases them, removes non-alphanumeric characters, and removes duplicates — the (u) makes it unique, (s: :) splits on spaces, and (L) lowercases.
explanations.138: This counts how many blog post files exist, then sets ceiling to one-tenth of that count (with a minimum of 3) — this filters out super-common words that appear in too many articles to be useful.
explanations.152: This counts the number of matching files by piping the list through grep -c . which counts non-empty lines, since $files is already a newline-separated list.
explanations.166: sed -n 's/^slug: *//p' finds lines starting with 'slug: ' and removes that prefix, printing only matches; head -1 takes the first one in case there are multiples, and the final sed strips surrounding quotes.
